blocks.text: Registering a resource is the moment you actually tell the SDK about something a client can read. Up to this point we have talked about what a resource is and how its URI is shaped. Now we write the code that makes one real.
This lesson walks through the registration call itself, the fields it needs, and the difference between a resource whose content never changes and one that computes its content fresh on every read.
By the end you will be able to register several resources cleanly in one server and confirm they show up correctly when a client asks for the list.
1. What Registration Actually Means
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440804349-218350889.png
Registering a resource means telling the SDK four things at once: what to call it, what URI identifies it, what kind of content it is, and what function produces that content.
The SDK stores this information internally. It uses it to answer resources/list and to route resources/read requests to the right handler.
Nothing is exposed to a client until you register it. An unregistered function is just a function, invisible to the protocol.
2. The Five Pieces Every Registration Needs

blocks.alt: The Five Pieces Every Registration Needs
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440804350-512119442.png
Every resource registration is built from the same five ingredients, no matter which SDK you use.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Purpose"],"rows":[["URI","The stable identifier a client will use to read this exact resource again"],["Name","A short human friendly label shown in resource lists"],["Description","A sentence explaining what the resource contains, helpful for a human or a model deciding whether to read it"],["mimeType","Tells the client how to interpret the bytes it gets back, text plain, application json, and so on"],["Handler","The function that actually produces the content when resources or read is called"]]}

blocks.text: Miss any one of these and the resource either fails to register or shows up confusingly in a client, so it is worth treating all five as required in practice.
Some SDKs allow extra optional metadata alongside these five, such as size hints, but the five above are the ones you should always plan for.
3. Registering a Static Resource
A static resource is the simplest case. Its handler always returns the same content, or content that only changes when you redeploy the server.
Here is a static resource in the TypeScript SDK, exposing a fixed readme file.
Notice the handler still runs code, it reads a file from disk, but the content it hands back is effectively fixed. The README does not depend on who is asking or when.
4. Registering a Dynamic Resource
A dynamic resource computes its content at the moment resources or read is called, so two reads a minute apart can return different answers.
Here is a dynamic resource in the Python SDK, exposing the current number of open support tickets.
The URI and name stay fixed across calls, only the returned value changes. That stability is exactly what lets a client keep re-reading the same resource meaningfully.
5. Static Versus Dynamic, Side by Side

blocks.alt: Static Versus Dynamic, Side by Side
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440804350-684484852.png
The registration call looks almost identical for both kinds. What differs is entirely inside the handler body.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Static resource","Dynamic resource"],"rows":[["Content per call","Same content every time","Recomputed on each read"],["Typical source","A file, a bundled constant, a fixed doc","A database query, an API call, a live measurement"],["Caching by client","Safe to cache aggressively","Should be re-read when freshness matters"],["Example","A README or a style guide","Open ticket count, current server load"]]}

blocks.title: Good to know
blocks.content: The SDK does not ask you to declare which kind a resource is. Static versus dynamic is purely about what your handler function does, not a separate setting.

blocks.text: 6. Why the mimeType Field Matters
The mimeType tells a client how to treat the bytes coming back, before it even looks at the content.
text/plain means plain human readable text. application/json means the client can parse it as structured data. text/markdown hints that formatting should be rendered.
Getting this wrong does not crash anything, but it can make a perfectly good resource display badly or get parsed incorrectly on the client side.
7. Description Is for Humans and Models Both
The description field is easy to treat as an afterthought, but it does real work.
A person browsing a resource list uses it to decide what to click. A model deciding whether a resource is relevant to a task reads the same description to decide whether to fetch it.

items: Say what the resource contains, not how it is implemented.
Mention if the content changes over time, so a reader knows whether to expect the same answer twice.
Keep it to one clear sentence, resource descriptions are meant to be scanned quickly.

blocks.text: A vague description like data or info tells a reader nothing useful, so it is worth spending the extra few seconds to write a real sentence.
8. The Handler Function Contract
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440804555-186887147.png
A resource handler receives the URI being read and must return content wrapped in the shape the protocol expects.
The contents array can hold more than one item, but in the common case it holds exactly one, matching the URI that was requested.
9. Handlers Can Do Real Work
A handler is an ordinary function, so it can read files, query a database, call another service, or run a computation.
The only rule is that it eventually returns content in the expected shape, whatever work happens before that is entirely up to you.
10. Organizing Many Resources Cleanly
A real server often exposes dozens of resources, so registering them all inline in one giant file quickly becomes hard to read.
A common pattern is grouping related resources into their own module and calling one setup function from the main server file.
11. Naming Resources Consistently
When many resources live in one server, a consistent naming style makes the list readable instead of confusing.

items: Use short lowercase names with hyphens, matching the style of your URIs.
Group related resources under the same URI scheme or authority.
Keep names distinct enough that two resources are never confused at a glance.

blocks.text: This effort pays off the moment a client shows a long resource list to a human or a model, both benefit from names that are easy to tell apart.
12. Avoiding Duplicate URIs
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440804556-349900943.png
Two resources registered with the same URI is a mistake the SDK usually will not catch for you automatically.
Whichever registration happens last tends to silently win, and the other one becomes unreachable, which can be a confusing bug to track down.

blocks.title: Watch out for this
blocks.content: When you split registrations across files, keep a shared list of URI prefixes per module so two modules never accidentally claim the same identifier.

blocks.text: 13. Testing That Registration Worked
The most direct way to confirm a resource registered correctly is to call resources or list and check it appears with the right fields.
A correct response includes your resource with the exact URI, name, description, and mimeType you set at registration time.
14. Testing the Handler Itself
Showing up in resources or list only proves registration happened, it does not prove the handler returns good content.
Follow up with a resources or read call using the same URI, and check the contents field matches what you expect.

items: Check the URI in the response matches the URI you requested.
Check the mimeType matches what you registered.
For a dynamic resource, call it twice and confirm the content can legitimately differ.
For a static resource, call it twice and confirm the content stays identical.

blocks.text: 15. Common SDK Gotchas
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440804556-409820213.png
A few small mistakes come up often enough to call out on their own.

blocks.text: 16. Registering Resources at Startup vs on Demand

blocks.alt: Registering Resources at Startup vs on Demand
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440804557-730879490.png
Most servers register every resource once, up front, when the server process starts, before any client ever connects.
That works well when the set of resources is known in advance, a fixed list of documents, a fixed set of database tables.
Some servers instead register resources as they discover them, for example scanning a folder at startup and registering one resource per file found.

items: Fixed set known in advance: register directly in your setup function.
Set discovered by scanning something at startup: loop over what you find and register one resource per item.
Either way, registration itself should finish before the server starts answering resources or list.

blocks.text: Worked Example
Suppose you are building a server for a small team wiki, and you want to expose both a fixed style guide and a live count of draft articles.
A client calling resources or list sees both entries with clean names and descriptions, with no visible clue about which one is static, exactly as it should be.
Common Mistakes

items: Skipping the description field because it feels optional, then wondering why nobody picks the resource in a list.
Hardcoding a mimeType that does not match the actual content being returned.
Registering two resources under the same URI without noticing one has become unreachable.
Writing a dynamic handler that is slow or unreliable, then being surprised when resources or read times out.
Scattering resource registrations across the codebase with no consistent grouping, making the server hard to navigate.
Forgetting to echo the requested uri back inside the contents array of the response.

blocks.text: Practice
Register two resources in a small MCP server: a static one exposing a fixed list of team holidays, and a dynamic one exposing the current server uptime.

Call resources or list and confirm both appear with correct URI, name, description, and mimeType. Then call resources or read on the dynamic one twice, a few seconds apart, and confirm the uptime value increased.
Key Takeaway
Registering a resource is one SDK call that binds a URI, a name, a description, a mimeType, and a handler function together.

Static and dynamic resources are registered the exact same way, the only difference is whether the handler returns fixed content or computes something fresh, and resources or list is your quickest check that registration actually worked.
